## Overview

Ligand–receptor-mediated (LRM) signaling inference requires defining which cell
pairs to score. When spatial coordinates are available, physical proximity
provides a principled basis for that definition. Without coordinates — as in
most droplet-based scRNA-seq experiments — the choice is less obvious.

The naive approach of scoring every possible cell pair is computationally
intractable: 14,000 cells produce nearly 200 million ordered pairs, each
requiring scores for hundreds of LRM pairs. More importantly, most of those
pairs are biologically uninterpretable because the cells never coexisted in the
same microenvironment.

NICHESv2's **sampled mode** solves this by drawing a stratified random sample
of cell pairs within each cell-type stratum. The sampling is reproducible (fixed
seed), keeps the cell-type composition of the data intact, and produces an edge
list compact enough for downstream analysis. The result is a `NICHESObject`
with the same slot structure as spatial mode, enabling identical downstream
workflows.

This vignette demonstrates the sampled-mode workflow using the
[`ifnb`](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat-data) dataset: ~14,000 PBMCs
profiled under control (CTRL) and interferon-beta stimulation (STIM) conditions,
annotated with 14 cell types.

---

## Setup

```{r libraries, eval=FALSE}
library(NICHESv2)
library(SeuratData)   # github.com/satijalab/seurat-data
library(SeuratObject)
library(ggplot2)
library(data.table)
```

Install and load the `ifnb` dataset if you have not done so already:

```{r load-ifnb, eval=FALSE}
# Run once to download (~50 MB)
# SeuratData::InstallData("ifnb")

data("ifnb")   # loads the Seurat object into your session
ifnb <- UpdateSeuratObject(ifnb)    # required: updates serialized object to current SeuratObject version
ifnb
#> An object of class Seurat
#> 14053 features across 13999 samples within 1 assay
#> Active assay: RNA (14053 features, 0 variable features)
```

---

## Step 1 — Ingest from Seurat

`extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat()` extracts the raw count matrix and cell
metadata from a Seurat object. It detects V4 and V5 assay structures
automatically, so no manual conversion is needed.

```{r extract, eval=FALSE}
inputs <- extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat(
  seurat.obj = ifnb,
  assay      = "RNA",
  layer      = "counts",
  verbose    = TRUE
)

dim(inputs$count.mtx)
#> [1] 14053 13999       # genes × cells

colnames(inputs$meta.data)
#> [1] "orig.ident"          "nCount_RNA"          "nFeature_RNA"
#> [4] "stim"                "seurat_annotations"
```

The `ifnb` metadata includes two columns we will use downstream:

- **`stim`** — experimental condition (`CTRL` or `STIM`); used as `sample.col`
- **`seurat_annotations`** — cell type labels (e.g. `CD14 Mono`, `CD8 T`);
  used as `cell.type.col`

```{r check-stim, eval=FALSE}
table(inputs$meta.data$stim)
#> CTRL STIM
#> 6548 7451
```

---

## Step 2 — Why sample splitting matters

The `ifnb` dataset contains cells from two independent conditions profiled in
separate batches. Constructing edges across conditions would pair a CTRL cell
with a STIM cell — a combination that never occurred in any biological sample.
Such cross-condition edges inflate apparent connectivity and make the results
uninterpretable.

Setting `sample.col = "stim"` instructs NICHESv2 to build edges **within**
each condition independently, then merge the resulting objects. Every edge in
the final NICHESObject is guaranteed to connect two cells from the same
condition.

```{r sample-splitting-note, eval=FALSE}
# Without sample.col: edges are built across all 13,999 cells simultaneously.
# CTRL cells can be paired with STIM cells — biologically meaningless.
#
# With sample.col = "stim": NICHESv2 processes CTRL (6,548 cells) and
# STIM (7,451 cells) separately, then merges. All edges are within-condition.
#
# Rule of thumb: if your experiment has multiple samples, donors, replicates,
# capture areas, or conditions, always set sample.col.
```

---

## Step 3 — Build the NICHESObject

```{r create-object, eval=FALSE}
niches.ifnb <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx     = inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data     = inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db        = load_LRM_database("fantom5", species = "human"),
  mode          = "sampled",
  species       = "human",
  sample.col    = "stim",
  cell.type.col = "seurat_annotations",
  method        = "product",
  n.cores       = 4L,
  verbose       = TRUE
)
```

`load_LRM_database("fantom5", species = "human")` loads the bundled FANTOM5
ligand–receptor database for human — no internet connection or additional
packages required.

---

## Step 4 — Inspect the result

```{r print-object, eval=FALSE}
print(niches.ifnb)
#> -- NICHESObject --------------------------------------------
#>   Cells        : 13999  (13999 non-empty)
#>   Genes        : 14053  (14044 valid)
#>   Edges        : 87957  (84637 non-empty)
#>   LRM pairs    : 820  (637 valid)
#>   Segmentation : none
#>
#>   Slot summary:
#>     $cell.list     -- character vector of cell barcodes
#>     $cell.data     -- (cell, gene, score, score.norm) [sparse]
#>     $cell.meta     -- per-cell metadata
#>     $edge.list     -- (edge, SendingCell, ReceivingCell)
#>     $edge.data     -- (edge, LRM, score, score.norm) [sparse]
#>     $edge.meta     -- per-edge metadata with Sending/Receiving/Joint cols
#>     $neighborhood.* -- reserved (NULL)
#>     $gene.list     -- character vector of gene names
#>     $gene.meta     -- per-gene metadata
#>     $LRM.list      -- character vector of 'ligand|receptor' pairs
#>     $LRM.meta      -- per-LRM metadata
#>     $segmentation  -- sf object of cell polygons, or NULL
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
```

Each **edge** is a directed cell pair (`SendingCell|ReceivingCell`). The
`$edge.data` slot stores LRM scores in sparse long format — only non-zero
signal is recorded:

```{r edge-data, eval=FALSE}
head(niches.ifnb$edge.data, 3)
#> Key: <edge, LRM>
#>                                 edge        LRM score  score.norm
#>                               <char>     <char> <num>       <num>
#> 1: AAACATACATTTCC.1|CGCACGGACTATGG.1 ANXA1|FPR3     6 0.008559201
#> 2: AAACATACATTTCC.1|CGCACGGACTATGG.1  B2M|HLA-F    95 0.135520685
#> 3: AAACATACATTTCC.1|CGCACGGACTATGG.1  CCL2|CCR1     6 0.008559201
```

The `$edge.meta` slot joins the cell metadata of both partners onto every edge.
Cell-type annotations propagate as `Sending.*`, `Receiving.*`, and `Joint.*`
columns:

```{r edge-meta, eval=FALSE}
head(
  niches.ifnb$edge.meta[, .(
    edge,
    Sending.seurat_annotations,
    Receiving.seurat_annotations,
    Joint.seurat_annotations,
    Joint.stim
  )],
  3
)
#> Key: <edge>
#>                                  edge Sending.seurat_annotations
#>                                <char>                     <fctr>
#> 1: AAACATACATTTCC.1|CGCACGGACTATGG.1                  CD14 Mono
#> 2: AAACATACCAAGCT.1|AAATTCGATAGACC.1                      CD8 T
#> 3: AAACATACCAAGCT.1|AAGGCTACAAGGGC.1                      CD8 T
#>    Receiving.seurat_annotations   Joint.seurat_annotations Joint.stim
#>                          <fctr>                     <char>     <char>
#> 1:                    CD14 Mono      CD14 Mono|CD14 Mono  CTRL|CTRL
#> 2:                           Mk                  CD8 T|Mk  STIM|STIM
#> 3:                            B                   CD8 T|B  STIM|STIM
```

---

## Step 5 — Pseudobulk connectivity

Single-cell edge scores can be aggregated to the cell-type level with
`compute_PseudoBulk_Connectivity()`. This function collapses expression to
pseudobulk profiles per cell type, scores all LRM pairs across all type–type
combinations, and returns a flat `data.table`:

```{r pseudobulk, eval=FALSE}
pb <- compute_PseudoBulk_Connectivity(
  count.mtx     = inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data     = inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db        = load_LRM_database("fantom5", species = "human"),
  cell.type.col = "seurat_annotations",
  method        = "product",
  n.cores       = 4L,
  verbose       = TRUE
)

dim(pb)
#> [1] 63858     7

head(pb[, .(SendingType, ReceivingType, LRM, score, score.norm)], 5)
#> Key: <SendingType, ReceivingType, LRM>
#>    SendingType ReceivingType           LRM        score   score.norm
#>         <char>        <char>        <char>        <num>        <num>
#> 1:           B             B  ADAM17|ITGA5 2.613739e-05 6.589340e-07
#> 2:           B             B  ADAM17|ITGB1 7.579845e-04 1.910909e-05
#> 3:           B             B ADAM17|NOTCH1 1.568244e-04 3.953604e-06
#> 4:           B             B  ADAM28|ITGA4 1.519733e-02 3.831306e-04
#> 5:           B             B   ADAM9|ITGA3  ADAM9   2.090992e-06 5.271472e-08
```

Note that `compute_PseudoBulk_Connectivity()` operates directly on the count
matrix and metadata — it does not require a `NICHESObject` as input. This
makes it straightforward to run as a standalone summary step before or
after sampled-mode inference.

### Visualising cell-type connectivity

To get a broad view of which cell types are most actively communicating,
aggregate `score.norm` across all LRM pairs and display the result as a
heatmap. The values are `log1p`-transformed before plotting because total
connectivity spans several orders of magnitude across cell-type pairs.

```{r heatmap, eval=FALSE}
# Sum raw scores across LRM pairs per type pair — score.norm is within-pair
# proportional and sums to ~1 per pair, making it unsuitable for cross-pair comparison.
pb.agg <- pb[, .(total.score = sum(score)),
             by = .(SendingType, ReceivingType)]

ggplot(pb.agg, aes(x = ReceivingType, y = SendingType,
                   fill = log1p(total.score))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "log1p(score)") +
  labs(
    title    = "Pseudobulk LRM Connectivity",
    subtitle = "ifnb dataset — FANTOM5 database",
    x        = "Receiving cell type",
    y        = "Sending cell type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid       = element_blank(),
    legend.key.width = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )
```

The heatmap rows are **sending** cell types and columns are **receiving** cell
types. Brighter tiles indicate higher aggregated normalised connectivity for
that directional pair across the full FANTOM5 LRM catalogue.

## What's next

This vignette covered the sampled-mode workflow for annotated scRNA-seq data
without spatial coordinates.

For spatially resolved data (Visium, MERFISH, Xenium, etc.), see the next
vignette: **Spatial-Mode Workflow**, which covers radius parameter selection
with `Explore_Radius_Neighborhood()`.
